summary:
Article 274 of Guinea's 2016 Penal Code punishes consensual same-sex conduct with six months to three years' imprisonment and a fine of GNF 500,000 to 1,000,000, or both. It replaced Article 325 of the 1998 Penal Code, which criminalised the same conduct through indecency provisions and set a lower minimum fine. Where violence or attempted violence is involved the sentence rises to five to ten years, and acts with a person under 21 carry the maximum penalty.

Police arrest on the basis of clothing and appearance, so exposure reaches people never charged with any conduct. Article 274 functions as a standing basis for extortion, and release is commonly secured by payment to officers. A 2024 Universal Periodic Review stakeholder submission reports LGBTQ people held for up to five days despite the 48-hour legal limit, most released only after paying bribes or fines.

Detention carries documented physical risk. LGBTQ people in custody are frequently abused. Transgender women are arrested and imprisoned on the stated pretext of protecting them from community violence, then held in male prisons where they often experience sexual violence. Security forces have arrested, harassed and used violence against LGBTQ people accused of disrupting social order. In 2016 and 2017 the organisation Afrique Arc-en-Ciel Conakry reported gay men jailed and fined for release.

In 2023 the Office for the Protection of Women, Children and Morals added a unit to investigate same-sex conduct, extending investigative machinery rather than protection. The 2024 Universal Periodic Review stakeholder reports describe an environment that is hostile and sometimes lethal, with threats of physical violence, and record that widespread stigmatisation hinders reporting of violence.

Guinea provides no legal gender recognition and no recognition of same-sex unions. No law protects LGBTQ people from discrimination in health services, and LGBTQ people face discrimination when seeking healthcare, housing, education and employment. In 2010 Prime Minister Lansana Kouyate stated that consensual same-sex activity was wrong and should be illegal and that sexual orientation should not be a human right.

Law L/2024/001/CNT/SGG of 12 January 2024 on HIV Prevention, Care, and Protection defines members of sexual minorities to include gays, lesbians, bisexuals, intersex and transgender people whether or not they self-identify, and Ordinance No. 056/2009/PRG/SGG on HIV/AIDS lists sexual minorities as a vulnerable and marginalised group. Neither instrument creates a non-discrimination guarantee in health services.

Section 9.9.30(b) of the Guinea Aeronautical Regulations (2022), issued by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, bars competent government agencies from using Passenger Name Record data that reveals an individual's sex life or sexual orientation alongside racial, ethnic, political, religious, trade-union or health data. The text gives no further detail on entry screening, visa rules or border checks for trans or LGBTQ travellers.

The US State Department's 2023 human rights report found that LGBTQ groups exist but cannot obtain legal recognition despite no law barring it, that most LGBTQ Guineans do not disclose publicly, that there is no substantial political presence of openly LGBTQ people, and that LGBTQ people are cast as part of a Western imperialist agenda attributed to the United States and France.
tangentialFactors:
A survey covering 2021 to 2023 found that 87 percent of Guineans would dislike or strongly dislike having a gay neighbor. The measure concerns gay neighbours rather than transgender people, and it records social attitude rather than incidence of violence.

Reporting on organised LGBTQ life differs across periods. The US State Department's 2011 report described homosexuality as socially, religiously and culturally taboo with no LGBTQ organisations in the country, while the 2023 report found that LGBTQ groups do exist but could not obtain legal recognition despite no law barring it.

The same 2011 report documents security-force torture, prison abuse and female genital mutilation, which sets the general custodial context in which LGBTQ detentions take place.
localsOnly:
Adoption is open to a couple married at least five years or to an unmarried person aged at least 30, subject to a 15-year age gap, and Guinean law does not specifically bar LGBTQ people from adopting.

Families arrange forced heterosexual marriages, and religious, cultural and familial pressure is used in attempts to make LGBTQ people conform to heterosexual lives, a pressure that falls heavily on younger people.

Some LGBTQ Guineans have been internally displaced to escape areas whose religious and cultural norms endanger them.
outOfScopeNotes:
The US State Department's 2023 report describes same-sex conduct as criminalised under Article 325 and its indecency provisions, while other sources in this record cite Article 274 of the 2016 Penal Code. Which article the 2023 report intended is unresolved here.

No source in this record addresses entry rules, visa conditions, gender markers in passports or identity documents, or airport and border screening treatment specific to transgender travellers. The 2022 aeronautical regulation on Passenger Name Record data is the only entry-adjacent provision sourced, and it gives no further detail.

No source addresses hate-crime provisions covering gender identity, restroom or facility access, or restrictions on gender-affirming healthcare. Whether such protections or prohibitions exist is not sourced.

No trans-specific violence or killing rate with a denominator appears in this record, so no comparison against Guinea's general homicide rate can be made.
